title: 3-Read Friday #30: Rehearsal in PD, Assessment Purpose, and Naked Explanation
author: Craig Barton
summary: Issue 30 closes out this batch with three picks Barton frames largely through his own professional evolution. His first, Peps Mccrea's "Rehearsal in PD," gets introduced as a personal conversion story: Barton admits he resisted rehearsal in coaching and CPD sessions for years, finding it a bit cringey, before it became the single biggest change he's made to his own practice, and he credits Mccrea's characteristically concise summary for capturing why it matters. His second pick, Jo Castelino's piece on rethinking assessment, is explicitly linked to the same changes theme, with Barton describing his own parallel shift toward treating tests as tools of learning rather than simply tools of assessment for both himself and his students. His third selection, Pete Foster's "Naked Explanation," gets a lighter, jokier introduction - Barton calling out the title as click-bait before reassuring readers their clothes are staying on - ahead of crediting Foster with a genuinely useful foreground/background framework for improving classroom explanations. The issue's throughline, more than most in the batch, is Barton narrating his own gradual changes of mind about coaching, assessment, and explanation.

quotes: The introduction of rehearsal has been the biggest change I have made to my coaching and CPD sessions. I resisted rehearsal for many years as I found it a bit cringey and didn’t see its purpose.
Now, I couldn’t imagine not including rehearsal. This summary from the ever-precise and concise Peps outlines the importance of rehearsal.
Regarding tests as tools of learning rather than simply tools of assessments was a big shift in mindset, both for me and my students.
In this post, Jo looks back at the reasons she used to give her students tests, and why she gives them now.
Here is a click-bait title if ever I read one. Fear not though, our clothes are staying on, as Pete looks at what we can do both in the foreground and in the background to improve our explanations.
